BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: On Wednesday, another low from the Gulf of Alaska will approach the coast with precipitation chances increasing late in the day.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Continued warm, dry days through Friday. Near record high temperatures.
- Valley rain and mountain snow along an eastward-moving cold front Friday night and Saturday morning. Additional rain and mountain snow, along with cooler temperatures, next week.
- Breezy south or southeast winds, strongest in Harney County Friday afternoon.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A strong upper level ridge over the interior western US will build further as the axis shifts eastward to the Continental Divide by late Thursday. Meanwhile, a Pacific upper trough will deepen as it moves eastward across the north Pacific. The highly amplified ridge/trough pattern will maintain warm, dry, and breezy weather in our CWA through Friday. High temps will be near daily records Thursday and Friday. Breezy east-southeast winds will blow in the Snake Basin between Boise and Twin Falls the rest of today, but lighter winds are expected Thursday. On Friday south winds will increase significantly in Harney County, with gusts to 45 mph. Southeast winds will also increase in the Snake Basin Friday afternoon with gusts to 30 mph. The Pacific trough will come inland Friday night and bring several hours of valley rain and mountain snow along an eastward-moving cold front. Latest models move the front across eastern OR Friday evening and western ID between midnight and 6 AM Saturday. Heaviest precipitation will be in the Boise Mountains -- up to .35 inch --, with .10 to .25 inch in other mountains, and .05 to .15 inch in the valleys. The frontal passage will end the gusty south winds in Harney County.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: will continue to move through the region and then east Saturday, with lingering precipitation ending gradually through the day behind the cold front. Winds will also remain breezy behind the front and gradually weaken in the evening. A brief upper-level ridge will make an appearance Sunday, creating dry and slightly warmer conditions from Saturday. The next system will be fast approaching late Sunday as a deep upper-level trough moves inland from the Gulf of Alaska. Winds will increase yet again late Sunday into early next week as this pattern moves in. This trough will also weaken as it moves over the area while still bringing a cold front and precipitation. While ensembles differ on the exact timing, it is expected to move through between Sunday night and early Tuesday, with Monday seeing the highest (50-80%) chances of precipitation. Light to locally moderate precipitation totals are expected. Snow levels will lower from around 6000 feet Sunday night to 4000-5500 feet by the time precipitation ends, allowing for additional mountain snowfall. Temperatures will trend lower with highs cooling to near normal by Tuesday. Winds will continue to weaken as the system progresses but remain locally breezy.
On Wednesday, another low from the Gulf of Alaska will approach the coast with precipitation chances increasing late in the day.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Our next system is progged to arrive sometime Wednesday. However, it is too soon to tell how exactly this disturbance will impact our forecast area, as model guidance varies greatly this far out.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions will prevail through Friday.
- Chances for rain and snow showers across the high country this weekend, with a few showers possible over the eastern plains.
- Another storm system possible early/mid next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: We are still on track for warm and dry weather through the end of the week as the axis of the upper level ridge shifts east over our area Thursday and Friday. On Thursday, expect mostly clear skies, with temperatures reaching mid-to-high 60s. However, Friday should be slightly "cooler" (low/mid 60s) as cloud cover will increase ahead of an incoming system.

An upper level shortwave will track across Colorado on Saturday before becoming a closed low over the Oklahoma/Texas panhandle by Sunday morning. This system will bring weak QG forcing and limited moisture into the region, mainly allowing mountain snow to fall Saturday and Sunday. Exactly how much snowfall is dependent on the strength of the system and moisture availability, but model trends have been consistent with light snow accumulations over the weekend. This could lead to minor travel impacts to high mountain passes as roads could become slick late Saturday and into Sunday morning. As for the plains, model guidance has continued to slowly back off on precipitation given the more southerly track of the system and overall lack of moisture transport into the region. This is congruent with the recent regional model outputs, with Lincoln county having the best chance for measurable precipitation Saturday night into Sunday. Portions of the eastern plains and Palmer Divide may still see a few light rain showers, but chances are pretty low (10-20%).

This weekend will also see a nice cooldown compared to this past week, with more seasonable temperatures arriving by Saturday. Expect highs to be in the mid 50s across the plains both Saturday and Sunday.

Monday and most of Tuesday should see a return of quiet weather as a weak upper level ridge shifts into Colorado. This will allow for a brief warm-up, but still expect temperatures in the high 50s, possibly reaching 60 F in the Denver metro area.

Our next system is progged to arrive sometime Wednesday. However, it is too soon to tell how exactly this disturbance will impact our forecast area, as model guidance varies greatly this far out. As of right now though, the mountains have a better chance receiving rain/snow showers out of this system than the plains. Will be keeping an eye on it. Looking farther out, ensembles favor the active weather pattern continuing.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: What once looked slightly more active and exciting has now started to look, well...dry and boring, as we move into the beginning of next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected to continue through the end of the week.
- Chances of precipitation increase over the weekend for the mountains, but remain low for the plains.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Benign weather is expected over the next few days as upper-level ridging slowly traverses the Rockies. Mild temperatures are forecast for both Thursday and Friday with 700 mb temperatures hovering around the 90th percentile for NAEFS climatology. Widespread highs in the 60s are expected for Thursday, which is 15 degrees above average for mid-November. The warm temperatures and sunny skies will make for a pleasant day across both southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska. Temperatures on Friday will dip a few degrees as more clouds float into the area ahead of a Pacific trough. Still looking at highs predominately in the 60s, but a few locations may drop into the upper 50s. Overnight lows both nights will remain on the warmer side as well, with temperatures in the 30s and upper 20s, which is 5 to 10 degrees above average. Besides temperatures, there is no real weather to speak of over the next 60 hours. Even the winds will be light under the ridge. The REFS does show low probabilities for fog developing in the Nebraska panhandle early Friday and Saturday morning as winds turn more southerly, but that will be ironed out with future model runs.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: This weekend will mark a transition period as a slightly more progressive pattern takes place after another week of anomalously warm and dry conditions. Saturday will start off much cooler than the previous day, as a cold front is expected to push across SE Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle during the morning hours. Not only will this result in forecast highs anywhere from 10-15 degrees cooler from the previous day, but northerly winds will increase as an inverted ridge sets up east of the Continental Divide. The increasing gradient flow as a result of a potent 1030 mb + anticyclone located over the Canadian Prairies will drive strong cold advection behind the front throughout the day, although no widespread precipitation is expected due to the main large-scale forcing being well to our south. While we certainly can't rule out some light snowfall especially within the Snowy and Sierra Madre Mountains, 50th percentile ECMWF ensemble QPF for SE Wyoming is currently sitting below 0.05" and has trended downward over the last couple of runs. This seems reasonable given that the primary shortwave trough and associated DCVA will be focused more over Southern Colorado.

GFS, Canadian, and ECMWF ensemble guidance are all in fairly good agreement that our region will be located in a region of upper-level diffluence on Sunday, downstream of an amplified trough located off the West Coast. This will place SE Wyoming and W Nebraska in a SW flow regime, with current LREF guidance suggesting PWAT values will situate as high as the 85th-95th percentile (0.4-0.5") relative to climatology. While this sounds great for us in desperate need of beneficial precipitation, mid and upper-level height rises associated with a building shortwave ridge, plus the lack of any forcing mechanism unfortunately point to mostly dry conditions. This is similar to much of what we have seen this fall given an active monsoonal pattern, yet we haven't been able to translate much of this moisture down to the surface as precipitation. Temperatures look to be at or slightly above average for this time of year, mainly in the low to mid 50s east of the Laramie Range, with slightly cooler to the west.

What once looked slightly more active and exciting has now started to look, well...dry and boring, as we move into the beginning of next week. The downstream ridge remains quasi-stationary over the Great Plains, whereas the upstream troughing begins to dig south and east towards Southern California. This will continue to SW surge of monsoonal moisture, which will unfortunately be confined primarily to the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere. As a result, SE Wyoming and W Nebraska will remain mostly dry and seasonably mild, with high temperatures on Tuesday and Wednesday 5 to 10 degrees above average for this time of year.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The wavy, unsettled pattern continues into next week. Models are indicating the potential for another round of mountain snow and valley rain in the Tuesday to Wednesday timeframe.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions and above normal temperatures will continue through the work week.
- Valley rain and mountain snow return to the forecast on Saturday favoring the southern mountains and adjacent foothills.
- An active weather pattern continues next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: UNSEASONABLY WARM AND DRY THROUGH FRIDAY:
High pressure will persist through the work week bringing unseasonably warm and dry conditions. Temperatures are expected to run 5-10 degrees above normal through Friday.

By Friday afternoon, high pressure will have moved east of the Divide, and flow aloft will shift southwesterly. This will begin to advect in rich subtropical moisture. A quick moving wave will track inland through the Great Basin Friday night into Saturday, acting on this rich moisture. Valley rain, mountain snow above 8k-9k feet, and an isolated thunderstorm or two are expected through the day Saturday. The highest probability of accumulating snow remains over the San Juans, generally above 10k feet. The likelihood of 6+ inches of snow for the San Juans remains high (70-80%), while the likelihood of 12 or more inches remains low (<20%). While the Central Colorado mountains are the next most likely areas to see accumulating snow of 6+ inches, the NBM probabilities keep that likelihood on the lower end (<30%). As high res guidance comes in over the next 24 hours, we'll get a better handle of snow totals and timing or greatest impacts. Slippery to hazardous travel will be possible over the mountains passes Saturday into Sunday. Snow levels are expected to drop to 6k-7k feet by Sunday morning, however the bulk of the precipitation will be over by then, with only lingering orographic showers expected. Temperatures through the weekend will run near-normal for mid- November.

The wavy, unsettled pattern continues into next week. Models are indicating the potential for another round of mountain snow and valley rain in the Tuesday to Wednesday timeframe. Confidence on the details of this potential system remains low, however, as a wide variety of solutions exist regarding the track, timing, and strength of this system.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Long-range guidance continues to suggest a broad trough moving over the western CONUS, with moisture pushing into our CWA sometime around late Tuesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mountain snow showers arrive Saturday-Sunday, with rain over the plains.
- After a brief lull through about Monday, models suggest more active weather mid-late next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Mild and dry conditions will persist across the area through the next 24 hours. Temperatures will be in the 50s-60s both today and tomorrow, with mostly clear skies and light winds.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Quiet weather will continue on Friday, with highs once again in the 50s-60s, with dry and mild conditions.

Starting on Saturday, the upper ridge over us will push east, with some energy moving through the Four Corners and into our forecast area. Though the day will start off mild and dry, moisture will push into the area from the west by late afternoon. This will kick off snow showers over the mountains first, with rain showers moving over the lower terrain by Saturday evening.

Latest data shows snow levels remaining around 8-9 kft, lowering towards 7 kft into early Sunday. Latest snow totals have risen a bit compared to previous estimates. The San Juans are now expected to receive widespread 3-5 inch accumulations, though localized amounts may rise as high as 8 inches. Models remain in decent agreement on the path of this quick-moving low, which has increased forecast confidence a bit, though totals are still expected to change as the system draws closer and is better resolved. So, no highlights needed quite yet. The rest of the central and southeast mountains will get much lighter snow, with most of the peaks getting less than 2 inches, though portions of the Sangres may see up to 3. Though, depending how quickly the system passes us by, it's possible some of the guidance may be overdoing totals slightly.
After a brief lull in activity Monday, with slightly warmer and drier conditions, a new system is expected to move in.

Long-range guidance continues to suggest a broad trough moving over the western CONUS, with moisture pushing into our CWA sometime around late Tuesday. However, the disagreement between model solutions remains substantial, so details have yet to be narrowed down. Generally cooler and unsettled weather expected around the middle of next week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: As the storm system exits the area Saturday night, high pressure will make a brief return, allowing for a quick break in the weather.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions with valley inversions persist through the end of the week before valley rain and mountain snow arrive this weekend that will help to mix out the inversions.
- Guidance continues to show two more storms next week, but details remain uncertain.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A high-amplitude ridge sits directly overhead this evening, maintaining dry and stable conditions with light winds. The ridge axis will slowly shift east on Thursday, bringing southerly flow aloft over Utah which will increase through Friday ahead of the next approaching storm system. Surface winds are not expected to realize the increased southerly flow on Thursday, but by Friday, as the surface pressure gradient increases over western Utah, there will be a greater chance of enhanced winds which, could help to improve mixing mainly west of I-15.

Said storm system, an open-wave trough with a bit of a negative tilt, is expected to move through Utah relatively quickly on Saturday, bringing widespread valley rain and mountain snow to the area. While some models show a few showers developing as early as Friday afternoon, ensemble means are focusing on the Friday night through Saturday evening timeframe as the most likely for precipitation. Latest NBM shows 25th percentile QPF values generally between 0.35 to 0.7 inches over the mountains and I-15 corridor (less elsewhere), with 75th percentile values of between 0.75 to over 1.25 inches over the same areas (0.25-0.7 inches elsewhere). Behind the cold front, with H7 temperatures falling to between -4 to -6C by the tail end of precipitation, snow levels down to between 6-7kft can be expected. Latest NBM 25th-75th percentile snow amounts range from generally 4-8 inches with locally higher amounts in the upper Cottonwoods.

As the storm system exits the area Saturday night, high pressure will make a brief return, allowing for a quick break in the weather. However, the pattern is progged to remain progressive, with another storm system impacting the area around the Tuesday/Wednesday timeframe. Some model spread regarding the timing and evolution of this system exists, with global deterministics mainly tying this to the extent of splittiness exhibited by the storm as it approaches Utah. Some models suggest that this storm will be associated with colder temperatures that could bring snow levels down to at least the higher valleys (5-6kt) and potentially lower, though the probability of measurable snow along the Wasatch Front valleys remains generally under 10%.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. Avoid isolated pockets of wind-drifted snow above treeline. Clear and warm days keep the possibility of wet, loose avalanches in the picture in the afternoon on sunny, south-facing slopes.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe for travel, with too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around firm, drifted snow below ridges or in gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has yet to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. Except on the steepest, highest-elevation, north-facing slopes, the mountains are snow-free. Avalanches will be unlikely until a deeper, layered snowpack builds. Once winter does arrive, even a small amount of snow with enough wind can create unstable avalanche conditions. If you're traveling in the mountains during or after a storm, be wary of steep, wind-loaded features at upper elevations and watch out for terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information as more snow accumulates
hazard_discussion: Due to a warm and dry fall season, the mountains in our forecast zones remain mostly dry, with little to no snow on the ground. As you're waiting for winter to arrive and the mountain snowpack to stack up, here are a few things to consider:
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Dylan Craaybeek
bottom_line: Generally safe avalanche conditions exist. The few spots where you may be able to trigger a slab avalanche are where you find wind-drifted snow on slopes facing the north half of the compass above treeline. Look for small cornices or a wave-like snow surface appearance to warn you there might be a cohesive slab of wind-drifted snow, and avoid traveling across those areas in steep, consequential terrain.
